repr(Rust)'s freedom to reorder fields is not a courtesy; the Reference explicitly declines to document the algorithm and reserves the right to change it between compiler versions, so any code that infers a field's position from its declared order, without checking, is relying on something the language never promised

items.item: The two source orders in step 1 happen to produce the same layout because the compiler's current heuristic (roughly: place larger-alignment fields first) already finds a minimal arrangement for this particular set of fields; a different set of field sizes could legitimately need a different one of the two orders to reach the same minimum

items.item: repr(C)'s fixed field order is exactly what makes it suitable for FFI and wire formats: a C compiler on the same platform lays the same field order out the same way, so repr(C) is the contract both sides can rely on, which repr(Rust) explicitly is not

at.step: repr(C): the same reorder, now it costs four bytes

items.item: The padding repr(C)'s Bad ordering inserts is not wasted by the compiler's choice; it is required by alignment itself — length (u16) can only start on an even address, and seq (u32) only on a four-byte boundary, so the padding is the minimum the alignment rules force once the order is fixed

at.step: repr(C): the same reorder, now it costs four bytes

items.item: offset_of! is resolved entirely at compile time and costs nothing at run time; it is syntactic sugar for a computation the compiler already has to do to lay the type out, exposed so a program (or a const assertion) can read it back

at.step: offset_of! and a compile-time assertion make the claim checkable

items.item: A const-context assert! is not the same mechanism as a run-time assert!: it is evaluated during the compiler's own constant-evaluation pass, which is why a false claim becomes error[E0080] at build time rather than a panic that only fires if that code path happens to execute

items.item: This topic's -Z randomize-layout demonstration needed a struct with eight fields, not the four-field header used elsewhere; a type with too few fields has too few valid orderings for alignment to allow, so the randomizer can end up picking the same one anyway, which would have looked like randomization not working rather than randomization having little room to use

at.step: -Z randomize-layout: the same struct, shuffled on purpose

items.item: The Unstable Book's own text is explicit that randomization isn't guaranteed to differ per compilation without -Z layout-seed providing extra entropy; this topic's examples.py therefore asserts on two different, fixed seeds rather than relying on two unseeded runs happening to differ

-Z randomize-layout is still gated behind nightly years after its tracking issue opened, which is itself informative: the Rust project has not judged the default layout algorithm stable or safe enough to randomize by default on stable, even though the whole point of the flag is to catch code that already shouldn't be relying on any one layout

Everything this topic measured is about one value's own layout, standing still; it says nothing yet about whether that layout is safe to read back from a byte buffer that came from somewhere else, where the padding bytes this topic showed are very much real and may never have been written at all

at.step: Recap: layout is the compiler’s choice, until you fix it
